title: The mandala offering
hook: offering the whole universe, pictured as a mandala of rice

segments.voice: Yesterday, ngondro, the four practices under everything else. Your line was the foundations. What basic thing held you up yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred six.

A small round plate, often brass or silver. A bowl of rice beside it. The practitioner wipes the plate in circles with the inside of the wrist, then lets rice fall in a ring, sets a smaller ring on top of that, then another, until there's a little stacked heap with an ornament on top. A verse is recited. Then the rice is tipped off, the plate is wiped, and it all begins again. From across the room it could pass for a child's game with dinner. In the practitioner's mind, it's the whole universe, being given away.
screen: `A PLATE, A BOWL OF RICE.` → `RINGS ON RINGS.` → `TIPPED OFF, BEGUN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Mandala is a Sanskrit word usually translated as circle. Here the circle is the world itself, ordered and complete, seen from above. Second, what the rice stands for. The offering draws on a picture of the cosmos found in Buddhist texts from India. At the center, a great mountain, Meru. Around it, continents and oceans, a sun and a moon, and every precious thing anyone could want. Each heap of rice stands in for a part of that world. So the little plate holds mountains, oceans, and everything in between. Third, why give the universe away. None of it is yours, and that's partly the point. Teachers explain the offering as a training in generosity with no ceiling. People often give what they can spare. Here the practitioner gives everything, beautiful things included, along with their own body and their own good deeds. Tibetan teachers count it among the ways of gathering merit, the goodness that ripens into a path. What gets lighter is the grip, the habit of holding on. Fourth, wiping the plate. Some teachers say the wiping is as much a part of the practice as the heaping: clearing the mind the way you clear the plate. And when the rice is tipped off, nothing is kept. The world is offered, emptied, and offered again. This offering isn't the colored-sand mandala some monasteries build and sweep away, though both share the word. It's a gift you can carry in two hands.
screen: `MANDALA: A CIRCLE, THE WORLD.` · `MOUNTAIN, CONTINENTS, SUN AND MOON.` · `GIVING WITHOUT A CEILING.` · `WIPED, EMPTIED, OFFERED AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer something small and whole. Rest your hands open on your lap, palms up. Bring to mind one thing that's complete and good in your world: a morning, a view, a person's laugh, the light in a window. Let it sit in your open hands the way the rice sits on the plate. Then, without sending it anywhere in particular, give it away. Let your hands stay open after. If something else good arrives, offer that too. If you are a Buddhist, you can offer it to the Buddha, the teaching and the community. The bell holds the time.
The mandala offering. The whole universe, pictured in heaps of rice on a round plate, and given away. Today's word.
Your line: the whole world offered. Today, give one thing away completely: a compliment with no angle, a seat, the last bite. Day one thousand three hundred six.

howItsDone: In the Tibetan foundational practices, students build and offer a mandala of rice on a round plate many times while reciting an offering verse, picturing the whole universe given to the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

options: keep it on the shrine as a treasure.
tip it off, wipe the plate, and offer again.
count the rice to see how much you gave.

original.note: Sanskrit mandala: usually translated circle; here, the whole world pictured as one round offering.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mandala is a pretty pattern.
what it means: in this practice, the whole universe pictured as heaps of rice on a round plate, and given away.
what a scholar hears: the cosmos of Indian Buddhist texts, Meru and its continents, used in the Tibetan preliminaries to gather merit by giving everything.

notes: Plate materials (brass or silver), wiping with the wrist, and stacked rings with a top ornament: described as common practice; details vary by lineage.
Offering of body and merit alongside the universe, and the offering as a way of gathering merit: confirm phrasing.
Wiping the plate as clearing the mind is attributed to 'some teachers'. Confirm.
Distinction from sand mandalas: confirm wording.
Editor pass: removed the unsourced historical claim that Buddhists 'inherited' an 'old' Indian cosmology; now tied to the Abhidharmakosha's cosmos as cited.
